newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon to unveil commercial plans later.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon to unveil commercial plans later.

text.p: Raytheon Co Chief Executive Dennis Picard said the defense giant will announce in about two months more specific plans on the future of its commercial businesses.

"At the present time, we are taking a hard look at the entire commercial business," Picard told reporters at a press conference in New York. "I think in approximately two months we will have more to say on that."
Picard hoped the merger with the defense electronics business of General Motors Corp unit, Hughes Electronics Corp, would add jobs on a net basis.
"Our hope is that, near-end, the amount of people we hire will offset the reductions we will have," Picard said.

Picard said some of the 127,000 employees with the new company, including the Texas Instruments Inc defense operations Raytheon bought earlier this month, will be cut or moved in a consolidation of some defense operations. But the combined companies have openings for 2,500 jobs.
"In the future, we're looking for growth and we're hoping we can neutralize the cuts we have to make because of the synergies," he said.
Picard said the merger will result eventually in cost savings of about 10 percent.

"We see great synergies. We feel there will be approximately a 10 percent reduction (in costs) over a period of time, most likely 2-1/2 years," Picard said. "The synergies...will enable us to offer to our customers, most importantly the U.S. government, significant cost savings and enhanced capabilities," he said.
The merger will raise materiel procurements by $7 billion and create opportunities for further savings, as well as the ability to cut research and development costs, he said.
Picard said he did not expect antitrust issues to cloud the proposed merger.
Hughes and Raytheon overlap in the area of missiles and radar, but Picard said the combined company was still at parity with another large competitor, which he did not name.
"We think that this will not be a problem," he said. "We have other examples where the combination just puts us in a position to compete," he added.
Picard, 64, said the board of directors asked him to stay on to oversee the merger with the Hughes and Texas Instruments defense operations.
He declined to say when he would step down or identify a likely successor.
